claim: Core symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder and other anxiety disorders include excessive fear and avoidance.
source: Core symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder and other anxiety disorders include excessive fear and avoidance (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to American Psychiatric Association, 2013

claim: The neural mechanisms of excessive fear have been well-characterized in rodents using Pavlovian fear conditioning.
source: The neural mechanisms of excessive fear have been well-characterized in rodents using Pavlovian fear conditioning (Johansen et al., 2011; Duvarci and Pare, 2014; Herry and Johansen, 2014; Giustino and Maren, 2015; Do Monte et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The mechanisms of active avoidance are just beginning to emerge.
source: yet the mechanisms of active avoidance are just beginning to emerge.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge in the field

claim: The prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and striatum are all necessary for the expression of active avoidance in rats.
source: Previous work in rats has shown that the prefrontal cortex, amygdala, and striatum are all necessary for the expression of active avoidance (Martinez et al., 2013; Moscarello and LeDoux, 2013; Beck et al., 2014; Jiao et al., 2015; LeDoux et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of the prelimbic prefrontal cortex (PL) impaired the expression of avoidance without affecting freezing.
source: Using a tone-signaled, platform-mediated avoidance task, we observed that pharmacological inactivation of the prelimbic prefrontal cortex (PL) impaired the expression of avoidance without affecting freezing (Bravo-Rivera et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study by the authors

claim: Avoidance that persisted following extinction was correlated with excessive PL activity, as indicated by the immediate early gene cFos.
source: Furthermore, avoidance that persisted following extinction was correlated with excessive PL activity, as indicated by the immediate early gene cFos (Bravo-Rivera et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior study by the authors

claim: PL activity may drive the expression of active avoidance.
source: suggesting that PL activity may drive the expression of active avoidance.
evidence: Speculative statement based on prior findings

claim: Fear conditioning mainly induces excitatory responses to conditioned tones in PL that correlate with freezing.
source: Fear conditioning mainly induces excitatory responses to conditioned tones in PL that correlate with freezing (Baeg et al., 2001; Burgos-Robles et al., 2009; Sotres-Bayon et al., 2012; Isogawa et al., 2013; Pendyam et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: The firing properties of PL neurons in active avoidance have not been studied.
source: but the firing properties of PL neurons in active avoidance have not been studied.
evidence: Statement about the gap in knowledge

claim: Muscimol (MUS) was confined to PL in its mid rostral-caudal extent.
source: Histological analysis showed that MUS was confined to PL in its mid rostral-caudal extent (Figure 1A).

claim: Rats with substantial spread of MUS to adjacent infralimbic cortex were excluded (n = 3).
source: Rats with substantial spread to adjacent infralimbic cortex were excluded (n = 3).
evidence: Statement about experimental exclusion criteria

claim: In some cases, MUS reached the ventral half of cingulate cortex (Cg1), and these cases were included due to similar functions of Cg1 and PL in conditioned fear and avoidance.
source: In some cases, MUS reached the ventral half of cingulate cortex (Cg1), and these cases were included due to similar functions of Cg1 and PL in conditioned fear (Courtin et al., 2014) and avoidance (Orona and Gabriel, 1983; Freeman et al., 1996).

claim: 2/13 rats never avoided following MUS infusion (Mann Whitney U Test, p<0.001).
source: and 2/13 rats never avoided (Mann Whitney U Test, p<0.001, Figure 1E).

claim: MUS increased tone-induced freezing (SAL = 36% vs. MUS = 55% freezing, t(28) = 2.460, p=0.020).

evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: MUS had no effect on suppression of bar pressing (SAL = 0.922 vs. MUS = 0.984 suppression ratio, t(28) = 0.194, p=0.848).
source: but had no effect on suppression of bar pressing (Figure 1E bottom inset; SAL = 0.922 vs. MUS = 0.984 suppression ratio, t(28) = 0.194, p=0.848).

source: Inactivation of PL had no effect on locomotion, as indicated by distance traveled during a 5 min open field test (SAL n = 10, 13.23 m vs. MUS n = 10, 12.53 m, t(18) = 0.513, p=0.614, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

source: Nor was there an effect on anxiety, as assessed with time spent in the center of the open field (SAL = 15.69 s vs. MUS = 18.76 s, t(18) = 0.933, p=0.363, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of PL delayed the expression of active avoidance.
source: Thus, pharmacological inactivation of PL delayed the expression of active avoidance.

source: Laser illumination significantly decreased the firing rate of 38/70 neurons and increased the firing rate of 9/70 neurons (Wilcoxon signed-ranks test comparing pre-laser vs laser activity of each unit using 1 s time bins, all p's <0.05).

source: Photosilencing also had no effect on the time course of avoidance in rPL (Figure 2E left) or cPL (Figure 2F left).

claim: There was no significant effect of photosilencing on freezing in rPL (t(30) = 1.939, p=0.062) or cPL (t(14) = 0.590, p=0.565).

claim: Photosilencing rPL neurons during early avoidance training (on day 2) significantly reduced tone-induced freezing (eYFP-control: 31% (n = 9) vs. eYFP-ArchT: 7% (n = 8), t(15) = 0.288, p=0.012).
source: However, photosilencing rPL neurons during early avoidance training (on day 2) significantly reduced tone-induced freezing (eYFP-control: 31% (n = 9) vs. eYFP-ArchT: 7% (n = 8), t(15) = 0.288, p=0.012, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: Excitatory activity of PL projection neurons does not appear to be necessary for avoidance behavior.

claim: Silencing rPL tended to facilitate avoidance, raising the possibility that avoidance signaling may involve rPL inhibition rather than excitation.
source: Instead, silencing rPL tended to facilitate avoidance (as indicated by the decrease in avoidance latency), raising the possibility that avoidance signaling may involve rPL inhibition rather than excitation.
evidence: Speculative statement based on experimental results

claim: Both excitatory responses (Z > 2.58, first 500 ms) and inhibitory responses (Z < −1.96, in the first or second 500 ms) to tone onset were observed in PL neurons.
source: Both excitatory responses (Z > 2.58, first 500 ms) and inhibitory responses (Z < −1.96, in the first or second 500 ms) were observed (Figure 3B right).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Out of 205 neurons, 30 were excited (14%) and 22 were inhibited (11%) at tone onset, relative to 10 s of pre-tone activity.
source: Out of 205 neurons, 30 were excited (14%) and 22 were inhibited (11%) at tone onset, relative to 10 s of pre-tone activity (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: There were no significant differences in the percentage of excitatory tone responses in the avoidance group compared to the naïve or fear conditioned groups (avoidance-trained: 30/205 (14%), naïve: 20/166 (12%), fear: 25/191 (13%), Chi Square = 0.547, p=0.761).
source: Surprisingly, there were no significant differences in the percentage of excitatory tone responses in the avoidance group compared to the naïve or fear conditioned groups (Figure 3D top right; avoidance-trained: 30/205 (14%), naïve: 20/166 (12%), fear: 25/191 (13%), Chi Square = 0.547, p=0.761).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Inhibitory responses occurred more frequently in avoidance-trained rats compared to naïve and fear conditioned groups (avoidance-trained: 22/205 (11%), naïve: 3/166 (2%), fear: 3/191 (2%), Chi Square = 22.545, p<0.001).
source: Inhibitory responses, however, occurred more frequently in avoidance-trained rats compared to the other two groups (avoidance-trained: 22/205 (11%), naïve: 3/166 (2%), fear: 3/191 (2%), Chi Square = 22.545, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: PL neurons showed excitation (n = 26/175; 15%) and inhibition (n = 16/175; 9%) at platform entry.
source: PL neurons showed excitation (n = 26/175; 15%) and inhibition (n = 16/175; 9%) at platform entry (Figure 3G left)

claim: Responses to platform entry represent sensory perception and/or motor responses rather than avoidance of threat.

source: The latency of inhibition showed no correlation with the latency of platform entry (r = 0.022, Pearson correlation, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).

claim: The inhibitory response in most cells preceded platform entry (88/133 cells) but was not correlated with the latency of platform entry (r = 0.078).
source: The inhibitory response in most cells preceded platform entry (88/133 cells) but was not correlated with the latency of platform entry (r = 0.078, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: Similar inhibition was observed in trials where the rat chose not to avoid (n = 107 trials).
source: In fact, similar inhibition was observed in trials where the rat chose not to avoid (n = 107 trials, dashed orange line in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).

claim: Inhibitory responses in PL appear to signal that shock can be avoided (an avoidance option), regardless of whether the rat chose to avoid on that trial.
source: Rather than signaling avoidance behavior, therefore, inhibitory responses in PL appear to signal that shock can be avoided (an avoidance option), regardless of whether the rat chose to avoid on that trial.

claim: All neurons showing inhibition to the tone were located in rPL (blue, n = 22), with none in cPL.
source: Further analysis revealed that all neurons showing inhibition to the tone were located in rPL (blue, n = 22), with none in cPL (Figure 3I–J).

source: Most inhibitory responses (n = 18/22) were brief, ending by ~10 s after tone onset, whereas a smaller proportion were sustained throughout the tone (n = 4/22, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).

source: Neurons showing inhibition reduced their firing rate from 6 to 2 Hz on average (Figure 3J)

claim: Photoactivation at 2 Hz had an even weaker effect, increasing the firing rate from 0.4 to 1.19 Hz on average.
source: Photoactivation at 2 Hz had an even weaker effect, increasing the firing rate from 0.4 to 1.19 Hz on average (Figure 4D–E).

claim: Photoactivation of rPL significantly reduced avoidance throughout the tone (repeated measures ANOVA, main effect (Group), F(1) = 18.642, p<0.001, interaction effect (Group x Time) F(9) = 1.156, p=0.326, post hoc, 3–30 s, all p's < 0.01).
source: Examination of the time course of avoidance showed that photoactivation of rPL significantly reduced avoidance throughout the tone (Figure 5D left; repeated measures ANOVA, main effect (Group), F(1) = 18.642, p<0.001, interaction effect (Group x Time) F(9) = 1.156, p=0.326, post hoc, 3–30 s, all p's < 0.01).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Photoactivation delayed avoidance in 7/14 rats and blocked avoidance entirely in 7/14 rats (Mann Whitney U test, p<0.001).
source: Photoactivation delayed avoidance in 7/14 rats and blocked avoidance entirely in 7/14 rats (Figure 5D right; Mann Whitney U test, p<0.001).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: Photoactivation had no significant effect on freezing or suppression of bar pressing in either rPL (freezing: t(21) = 1.121, p=0.275; suppression: t(21) = 1.343, p=0.194) or cPL (freezing: t(14) = 0.0702, p=0.494; suppression: t(14) = 0.483, p=0.636).
source: Photoactivation had no significant effect on freezing or suppression of bar pressing in either rPL (Figure 5D insets, freezing: t(21) = 1.121, p=0.275; suppression: t(21) = 1.343, p=0.194) or cPL (Figure 5E insets, freezing: t(14) = 0.0702, p=0.494; suppression: t(14) = 0.483, p=0.636).

claim: Photoactivation at 2 Hz had no effect on avoidance expression.
source: Photoactivation at 2 Hz had no effect on avoidance expression (Figure 5F).

source: Thus, the photoactivation-induced impairment of avoidance showed specificity with respect to location, time, and frequency.

source: Finally, reducing the duration of 4 Hz photoactivation to the first 15 s of the tone delayed, but did not prevent, avoidance as indicated by time on platform (Figure 5H left; Mann Whitney U test, p's <0.05 at 9–15 s) and avoidance latency (Figure 5H right, t(17) = 3.363, p=0.004).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5H

claim: 4 Hz photoactivation of rPL had no effect on locomotion, as indicated by distance traveled in an open field (eYFP-control n = 11, 2.71 m vs. ChR2-eYFP, n = 15, 2.25 m, t(24) = 0.941, p=0.356).
source: 4 Hz photoactivation of rPL had no effect on locomotion, as indicated by distance traveled in an open field (eYFP-control n = 11, 2.71 m vs. ChR2-eYFP, n = 15, 2.25 m, t(24) = 0.941, p=0.356, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

source: Nor did it have any effect on anxiety levels, as assessed by time spent in the center of the open field (eYFP-control = 2.6727 s vs. eYFP-ChR2 = 2.6733 s, t(24) = 4.82e-4, p=0.999, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: Preventing inhibition in rPL glutamatergic neurons severely impaired avoidance expression.
source: Thus, preventing inhibition in rPL glutamatergic neurons severely impaired avoidance expression.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental data presented

claim: Optogenetic silencing of rostral PL accelerated avoidance.
source: Whereas pharmacological inactivation of PL delayed avoidance, optogenetic silencing of rostral PL accelerated avoidance.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental data presented

claim: Avoidance training was associated with inhibitory, rather than excitatory, tone responses in rostral PL neurons.
source: Single-unit recordings revealed that avoidance training was associated with inhibitory, rather than excitatory, tone responses in rostral PL neurons.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental data presented

claim: Opposing tone-induced inhibition by optogenetically activating rPL neurons delayed or prevented avoidance.
source: Consistent with this, opposing tone-induced inhibition by optogenetically activating rPL neurons delayed or prevented avoidance.
evidence: Summary statement based on experimental data presented

claim: Inhibition within PL is key for conditioned behavior.

claim: Lesions or inactivation of PL reduces freezing in Pavlovian fear conditioning tasks.
source: Previous work has shown that lesions or inactivation of PL reduces freezing in Pavlovian fear conditioning tasks (Baeg et al., 2001; Vidal-Gonzalez et al., 2006; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).

claim: There was no reduction in freezing following pharmacological or optogenetic inhibition of PL in the platform-mediated avoidance task.
source: In our platform-mediated avoidance task, however, there was no reduction in freezing following pharmacological or optogenetic inhibition of PL (present study; Bravo-Rivera et al., 2014).

claim: PL activity is no longer necessary for freezing following avoidance training.
source: Thus, PL activity is no longer necessary for freezing following avoidance training.

claim: It is unlikely that inhibitory responses in PL promote avoidance by decreasing freezing.
source: It is therefore unlikely that inhibitory responses in PL promote avoidance by decreasing freezing.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results

claim: Freezing levels increased following MUS inactivation, consistent with loss of avoidance as a possible response to the tone.
source: In fact, freezing levels increased following MUS inactivation, consistent with loss of avoidance as a possible response to the tone.
evidence: Inference based on experimental results

claim: Early stages of avoidance training depend on Pavlovian conditioning (acquisition of tone-shock association), whereas later stages of training shift to instrumental learning (platform entry).
source: It is well-established that early stages of avoidance training depend on Pavlovian conditioning (acquisition of tone-shock association), whereas later stages of training shift to instrumental learning (platform entry; Mowrer and Lamoreaux, 1946; Kamin et al., 1963; LeDoux et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: A decrease in freezing was observed following optogenetic silencing of PL early in avoidance training.
source: In agreement with this shift, we did, in fact, observe a decrease in freezing following optogenetic silencing of PL early in avoidance training.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented

claim: Excitatory responses to platform entry are consistent with prior cFos studies showing that active avoidance is correlated with increased PL activity.
source: Excitatory responses to platform entry are consistent with prior cFos studies showing that active avoidance is correlated with increased PL activity (Martinez et al., 2013; Bravo-Rivera et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: rPL inhibition is a training-induced property of the tone, indicating that shock is avoidable and that the rat has the option to avoid.
source: Instead of signaling avoidance behavior, we suggest that rPL inhibition is a training-induced property of the tone, indicating that shock is avoidable and that the rat has the option to avoid.

claim: 'Avoidability' in this task resembles 'controllability' when rats learn that they can terminate a shock by running in a wheel.
source: 'Avoidability' in this task resembles 'controllability' when rats learn that they can terminate a shock by running in a wheel (Maier and Seligman, 1976; Maier, 2015).

claim: Rats' control of shock reduced the activation of serotoninergic neurons in the dorsal raphe, a phenomenon blocked by PL inactivation.
source: In that task, rats' control of shock reduced the activation of serotoninergic neurons in the dorsal raphe, a phenomenon blocked by PL inactivation (Amat et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Inhibition in PL may reduce its effects on target structures such as the raphe, thereby signaling avoidability/controllability in a variety of contexts.
source: Thus, inhibition in PL may reduce its effects on target structures such as the raphe, thereby signaling avoidability/controllability in a variety of contexts.

claim: 4 Hz approximates the average firing rate of mPFC putative projection neurons.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The impairment in avoidance with 4 Hz stimulation was likely due to abolishment of inhibitory responses.
source: the impairment in avoidance was likely due to abolishment of inhibitory responses.

source: Excitatory responses coupled with the loss of inhibitory responses to the tone would cause PL responses in avoidance-trained rats to resemble those in fear conditioned rats, indicating that the shock is not avoidable.

claim: MUS inactivation would non-specifically inhibit all neuronal types and may resemble 4 Hz photoactivation by preventing any further inhibition at tone onset.
source: Whereas MUS inactivation would non-specifically inhibit all neuronal types, it may resemble our 4 Hz photoactivation by preventing any further inhibition at tone onset.

claim: Neurons in PL project to the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and ventral striatum (VS), both necessary for active avoidance.
source: Neurons in PL project to the basolateral amygdala (BLA) and ventral striatum (VS; Sesack et al., 1989; Vertes, 2004), both necessary for active avoidance (Darvas et al., 2011; Bravo-Rivera et al., 2014; Ramirez et al., 2015; Hormigo et al., 2016).

claim: Inhibition of excitatory inputs from rPL to VS may be permissive for avoidance behavior, which would resemble inhibition of VS during food seeking.
source: Inhibition of excitatory inputs from rPL to VS may be permissive for avoidance behavior, which would resemble inhibition of VS during food seeking (Rada et al., 1997; Saulskaya and Mikhailova, 2002; Do-Monte et al., 2017).
